problem: Open-vocabulary mobile manipulation systems fail not from semantic misunderstanding but from mismatch between symbolic plans and the evolving physical world: they rely on pre-scanned semantic maps that go stale, choose navigation endpoints without checking manipulation feasibility ('arrived but inoperable'), and use undifferentiated global replanning for anomalies.
motivation: Home-service robots must execute long-horizon tasks with open-set object references under frequent disturbances. Failures are dominated by execution inconsistency rather than language understanding. Aligning symbolic reasoning with verifiable physical state and containing failures locally should raise robustness.
key_idea: Close the loop between symbolic planning and physical state by anchoring predicates to observable geometry, choosing operability-aware base poses, and recovering at the minimum responsible layer.
insight: Per the abstract, explicit physical grounding and structured failure containment are what drive robustness. Task success rises from 53.3% to 71.7% in 60 real-robot trials, with a 71.4% recovery rate under perturbations. Only the abstract was available, so no ablations can be cited.
method: Physically anchored task planning: binds symbolic predicates to observable geometric anchors and re-validates them after each action.
Operability-aware base alignment: ensures navigation endpoints satisfy kinematic reachability and local collision feasibility for the downstream manipulation.
Minimum-responsible-layer hierarchical recovery: localizes failures across perception, base-arm coordination, and execution layers to prevent cascading retries.
